en: But I have found a door to the unconscious
that shows it clearly in healthy people, too.
That door is "the dream."
All sorts of everyday sights appear in dreams.
But they are often put together differently
from how they are in reality.
Yes, like actors cast in a stage play,
everyday scenes don't stand for real events;
they are merely used in a different story.
During sleep, when consciousness fades,
the unconscious tries to fulfill some wish,
just as it does in the symptoms of neurosis.
Now, do not misunderstand me.
I am not saying that dreams hold omens
or foretell the future. We can leave such
talk to quack fortune-tellers.
What I mean is that a dream is some "desire"
from the unconscious, emerging in altered form.
Then, if we operate on it with the scalpel
of proper interpretation, we can surely
come to understand the unconscious.
Yes, just as in treating neurosis.
Will you present it at this conference?
note: Stern register player (gentle parallel #2269 in msg 72230).

en: No, not yet.
I'm writing a book on it, but it seems
it will take a little more time.
It will come out as "The Interpretation of Dreams," without fail.
note: Freud's Die Traumdeutung; real English title.

en: I do hope you will read it.
I am confident in "The Interpretation of Dreams."
It will go beyond neurology and medicine
to influence every field of science.
Ah, it's you.
, it's you.

en: A paper?
so you would do well to read it.
Your keenness is commendable, but
come to Vienna sometime.
Hm? Are you attending the coming conference too?
<Yes, I am>
<No, I'm not>
You carry yourself calmly, and you seem
intelligent. You might understand it better
than the hidebound men at the conference.
do read it yourself some time.
I'm sure you can see how it differs
from quack psychotherapy.
Have you read the book?
I barely touched on it in that theory, but
I have found that beyond sexual matters,
something governs the depths of the mind.
Something governing the depths of the mind?
Yes.
Let me give you an example.
Recently, in his address opening Parliament,
the chair said "I declare Parliament closed"
by mistake.
Why did he make such a slip? Have you
any idea?
Because the words "open" and "closed"
are similar
But that alone does not explain it.
This is a man who presides over Parliament.
Unless something is badly amiss, he would
not make a mistake like that.
In fact, that session of Parliament had a great
many awkward items on its agenda.
It seems that since the day before, he had
been longing: "I want this session closed,
and soon."
Of course, in an address opening Parliament,
he could hardly say such a thing.
Yet his wish was fulfilled, by way of a
"slip of the tongue," without his knowing it.
Through some force or other.
Some force?
For now, I call it
"the unconscious."
